title: Who knew we would be obsessed with this screen?
author: engineering-AF7
selftext:
What are some things you are doing to control token spend? 

On my end, for repetitive complex tasks I am using Fable to come up with the result I want and to create the skill.  I then downgrade to a lower model to run the skill. 

https://preview.redd.it/ugtsidwngedh1.png?width=930&format=png&auto=webp&s=20b0de12383025091d3d0c7564ead49c7c213bb2

comments.author: magus_prime_x
comments.body:
I always keep the chat compact and avoid carrying unnecessary context for too long. 
For research, file searching, and early planning, I use a lower-cost model.
 Once the plan is complete, reviewed, and confirmed, I switch to the stronger model for the actual execution.

I also use at least two strong AI tools instead of expecting one to handle everything. 
For example, Claude can handle deep planning, visual judgment, documentation, and long project reasoning, while Codex can focus on coding, debugging, testing, and working directly inside the project or vice versa. 

Having one AI review the other’s work is also a great way to catch mistakes.
The prompt itself needs to be very specific: where the project is located, which files and folders it should work in, exactly what the task must do, what must not be changed, and which skills, tools, MCPs, or plugins it should use. I also include clear acceptance criteria so the AI can test its own work instead of guessing whether it is finished.

For bigger tasks, I split the work into focused stages: inspect first, create a plan, confirm it, execute, test, and verify. 
This usually gets the task completed properly within two or three attempts instead of wasting tokens through endless trial and error. If it still fails after that, I stop and investigate the root cause rather than repeating the same prompt.

replies.author: engineering-AF7
replies.body: Thank you, that is very helpful. The concept of for example having Fable in Claude Code create a plan and the let the very capable, but significantly cheaper GPT 5.6 implement it within Codex is something I will try.

comments.author: LiveBeyondNow
comments.body: A small tip ( aside from useful suggestions Magnus has) I use is to query a cheap model with a very small request. If you have a necessary query, even better, but the point is to start the 5hr clock about 2hrs before you “sit down to work”, that way your 5hr limit is reset sooner.  This doesn’t help with the weekly limits but I have also seen them not start until queried so I try to do the same on weekly resets.

comments.body: I use fable to plan and spec then sonnet 5 to execute, then fable to review.

comments.author: Forexcalibur
comments.body:
I create slash commands called /endsession and /remember.  When the session has accomplished its work, the session covers a lot of ground, I’m at a good stopping point, or approaching compaction, I run /endsession and it updates claude.md, status.md, memory, and session handoff, including anything that future sessions will need to come fully back up to speed with context, makes sure everything is committed, and pushes to the remote git repo.  /endsession has instructions to keep the .md files small and organize subject-specific guidance and guardrails into downstream .md files the root files reference.

After that I /clear to clear the session, and then run /remember, which causes Claude to read up all of the aforementioned files, verify state, review the previous session’s transcript, and come fully back up to speed with context.

I regularly run these slash commands while I’m working to keep my sessions accurate with lean, sharp, recent, relevant context.

replies.author: engineering-AF7
replies.body: Thank you, I will try this immediately.

replies.author: Forexcalibur
replies.body: Cool!  I’ll sanitize the slash commands to remove my stuff and paste them below for your reference.

replies.author: Forexcalibur
replies.body: Sure thing.  Good luck!  Obviously if the project doesn’t have a git repo, or your workflow is different you can ignore all that part, etc.

replies.author: Forexcalibur
replies.body:
/endsession

\---  
description: Capture the session into memory, handoff, and live-state docs so the next session resumes cleanly  
\---

You are closing out the current working session. Your job is to make the  
project's persistent state — memory, session handoff, and documentation —  
accurately reflect everything that happened, so a brand-new session (with  
zero conversation history) can run \`/remember\` and be fully up to speed.

Work through these steps in order. Do not skip steps; if a step has nothing  
to record, say so explicitly rather than silently omitting it.

\## 1. Commit + push the session's changes

Invoking this command is itself the operator's explicit consent to commit  
and push — do not ask again. Goal: end with a clean working tree and the  
remote in sync, so anything built or deployed this session maps to a real  
commit.

1. \*\*Inspect.\*\* \`git status --short\` and \`git log --oneline -10\`. If  
   already clean and in sync, say so and skip ahead.  
2. \*\*Triage\*\* into three groups: tracked+modified session-relevant files  
   (almost always commit); untracked session-authored repo-worthy files  
   (new tests, modules, docs — commit); scratch/cache/binaries/pre-existing  
   strays (do NOT commit). ⚠ Watch for \*\*tracked-under-ignored-path\*\* files  
   (canonical docs force-added under a gitignored directory): they need  
   \`git add -f\`, and combining a forced add with a normal add in one command  
   can abort the whole add — stage forced files in their own call.  
3. \*\*Scope\*\* the committable files into multiple tight, narratively-scoped  
   commits (mirror the repo's existing message style; check  
   \`git log --oneline -20\`) — one commit per logical change, plus a final  
   \`docs:\` commit for live-state/doc updates.  
4. \*\*Commit\*\* each group. Let hooks run (never \`--no-verify\`); never amend.  
5. \*\*Push\*\* once at the end. If it fails, diagnose — never force.  
6. \*\*Self-consistency.\*\* The docs written in later steps will reference  
   these commit hashes; if that creates drift, add a small follow-up  
   \`docs:\` commit — never amend.

If the session was purely conversational, state that and move on.

\## 2. Take stock of the session

Review the entire conversation. Enumerate: code/infra changes (commits with  
hashes, deploys, external resources created/modified/terminated); decisions  
made and the reasoning (including things explicitly deferred or rejected);  
lessons learned and guardrails (anything that surprised you, broke, or that  
the operator corrected); reference information a future session would need  
(IDs, paths, run-ids, URLs, costs); and unfinished work with its next action.

\## 3. Diff against the current docs

Compare what happened against \`CLAUDE.md\`, \`STATUS.md\` (or the project's  
live-state doc), and the relevant downstream docs (\`docs/\`,  
per-subdirectory \`CLAUDE.md\` files, \`memory/\`). Identify every place they  
are now stale, wrong, or missing information.

\## 4. Update the live-state docs

\- \*\*\`STATUS.md\`\*\* (or the project's live-state doc): update sections IN  
  PLACE (never stack dated banners); keep it a small snapshot, pushing  
  dated narrative to the changelog.  
\- \*\*\`docs/changelog.md\`\*\*: ONE dated entry per shipped change, newest first.  
\- \*\*\`CLAUDE.md\`\*\*: rules and pointers only — touch it only if a rule  
  changed; it carries no live state and no dated banners.  
\- \*\*Downstream docs\*\*: update anything whose subject changed; register new  
  docs in whatever doc index/registry the project keeps; archive superseded  
  docs with a tombstone rather than deleting.  
\- Run the project's doc linter/validator if it has one; fix errors you  
  introduced (report-only for pre-existing ones — never let lint block the  
  close).

\## 5. Write the session handoff

Write (or update, if one exists for today) a dated handoff memory file at  
\`memory/session\_handoff\_YYYY\_MM\_DD.md\`, with the standard memory  
frontmatter (\`name\`, \`description\`, \`metadata: type: project\`). Cover:  
commits (with hashes, noting pushed status), what shipped vs what is only  
built, decisions, the explicit NEXT ACTION, parked/deferred items, gotchas  
reconfirmed, and anything left uncommitted. Open with a pointer to the  
previous handoff.

\*\*The handoff's job is RESUMABILITY, not just a changelog.\*\* Beyond the bare  
facts it MUST include:

\- \*\*The mental model / WHY\*\* — what you're ultimately trying to achieve, why  
  the current thread matters, and the chain of reasoning to the next step,  
  including dead ends ruled out and why.  
\- \*\*A resume checklist\*\* — the literal first 2–4 actions for next session,  
  in priority order, naming exact files/commands so nothing is re-discovered.  
\- \*\*In-flight & scheduled state\*\* — anything backgrounded or detached, any  
  scheduled job (id, when it fires, what it writes), any live experiment and  
  where output lands, any "waiting on X" gate with its date/condition.  
\- \*\*Falsified hypotheses & why\*\* — what was tried, the result, and the  
  reason it failed (the reason often reshapes the next attempt). The next  
  session must not re-run a dead end.  
\- \*\*Exact artifacts on disk\*\* the next step consumes (data files, logs,  
  scratch harnesses to reuse) so iteration is cheap.

If the session had two distinct arcs, structure the handoff so each arc's  
resume state is self-contained. If run twice in one session, UPDATE the same  
dated file in place — refresh the NEXT ACTION and state-at-close so they  
never reflect a stale mid-session snapshot.

\## 6. Update the memory store

One file per fact in \`memory/\`, with the standard frontmatter (\`name\`,  
\`description\`, \`metadata: type: user|feedback|project|reference\`). \*\*Add\*\* a  
memory for each durable lesson, guardrail, gotcha, or reference worth  
keeping beyond this session — but not what the repo, git history, or  
CLAUDE.md already capture. \*\*Update\*\* memories this session proved  
incomplete (prefer editing over near-duplicates). \*\*Delete\*\* memories proved  
wrong. Maintain \`memory/MEMORY.md\`: one-line pointer per memory, mirrored  
into subject sub-indexes if the project keeps them. Keep the index itself  
small: the "resume here" section holds only the newest handoff as a  
paragraph plus at most one previous — collapse older entries to single  
lines in a dated handoff index.

\## 7. Report

Finish with a concise summary: files created/updated/deleted, and confirm in  
one sentence that the NEXT ACTION is recorded in the handoff.

replies.author: Forexcalibur
replies.body:
/remember

\---  
description: Read memory, the latest handoff, and the doc hierarchy to come up to speed and resume work  
\---

You are resuming work on this project in a fresh session with no prior  
conversation history. Your job is to reconstruct an accurate picture of  
where things left off, so you can pick up exactly where the last session  
ended — without re-asking the operator things the record already answers.

Work through these steps in order.

\## 1. Read the memory index

Read \`memory/MEMORY.md\` (or wherever the project keeps its memory index —  
the one small file loaded each session, pointing at the individual memory  
files). Note which entries look relevant to recent work.

\## 2. Read the latest session handoff

Find the most recent dated handoff file in the memory directory (e.g.  
\`memory/session\_handoff\_YYYY\_MM\_DD.md\`) and read it in full — it is the  
"read first" record and names the NEXT ACTION. If it references an earlier  
handoff or an active-plan memory for unfinished context, read those too.  
Follow links into any memory file that is clearly load-bearing for the  
current work.

\## 3. Read the live-state docs

\- \*\*\`STATUS.md\`\*\* (or the project's live-state doc) — the single source of  
  truth for what is deployed/running/in-flight right now.  
\- \*\*\`OPERATIONS.md\`\*\* (or the project's ops doc), if one exists — check any  
  calendar/recurring items: is anything due today? Note them in your briefing.  
\- \*\*\`CLAUDE.md\`\*\* — rules and the system map.  
\- Any per-subdirectory \`CLAUDE.md\` relevant to where work left off.

\## 4. Drill into the relevant subject docs

Based on what the handoff says is in flight, read the specific docs under  
\`docs/\` that the next action touches (the handoff and CLAUDE.md link to  
them). Do not read everything — read what resuming the next task requires.

\## 5. Verify before trusting

Memory and docs reflect what was true when written. If the record names a  
specific file, function, flag, commit, revision, or external resource you  
are about to act on, verify it still exists / still holds (e.g. \`git log\`,  
\`git status\`, a read-only API/describe call) before relying on it. Surface  
any drift you find between the record and reality.

\## 6. Report

Give the operator a concise briefing:  
\- Where things stand (current state, what shipped last).  
\- What is in flight or parked.  
\- The explicit NEXT ACTION from the handoff.  
\- Any drift you found between the record and reality.

Then ask whether to proceed with that next action, or wait for direction.
